text: Order breakfast in a Singapore kopitiam and it arrives in a form that has barely changed in a century: two soft-boiled eggs cracked into a saucer, with dark soy sauce and a shake of white pepper; kaya toast; and a cup of kopi or tea.

They are steeped: room-temperature eggs go into a covered pot or enamel mug, boiling water is poured over them, and they sit in the falling heat — home cooks time it at anything from five and a half to ten minutes, depending on the vessel — until the whites are just set and the yolks still run.
The two-egg serving is a documented custom with no documented origin, which may be the most Singaporean thing about it: it does not need a reason, because it has always been done this way.

Loi Ah Koon arrived from Hainan in 1926, aged fifteen, worked as a coffee-stall assistant, and set up his own stall at Telok Ayer Basin; the business was formally registered in 1944 — the year Ya Kun still prints on its signs.
Ya Kun has since gone international — the same set is served from Jakarta to Tokyo.
One Tokyo outlet opened in 2021 in the Kasumigaseki Building (it has since closed), and that building carries a personal footnote: it is where I once worked, during my AOTS time in Japan.

A decade later, in 1968, the American Heart Association issued the recommendation that started the egg's exile: less than 300 milligrams of dietary cholesterol a day, and no more than three whole eggs a week.

Two kopitiam eggs deliver somewhere between 372 and 480 milligrams — which is to say, the traditional serving, eaten before nine in the morning, meets or exceeds the entire day's allowance on its own.
In 2020 a BMJ analysis of three cohorts and a meta-analysis covering 1.72 million people found no association between eating at least one egg a day and cardiovascular disease at all.
Through all of it, Singaporeans went on ordering the two eggs — on the Board's own numbers, a single breakfast saucer holds more than a whole day's advised cholesterol.
The kopi-o has not been banned, taxed or portioned by the week; it has been graded, and the grading points at the spoon, not the bean.
The only thing that has ever actually removed the two eggs from the saucer was not a guideline.
The lesser-known thing is not that the two eggs survived the scare.
It is that nobody ever decided they should.
